# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging` (`mod.rs`)

# Bugs / Verification Blockers: `PageAligned` (hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.rs)

## VERUS-TOOL-1 — Verus panic verifying a generic trait impl whose trait method has `#[verus_spec]`

- **Type**: Verus tool limitation (not a Nanvix code bug). Recorded, not auto-fixed.
- **Symptom**: Marking `impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T>` with
  `#[verus_verify]` makes Verus panic during compilation:

  ```
  thread 'rustc' panicked at vir/src/traits.rs:511:13:
  assertion failed: !method_impls.contains(&p)
  ...
  vir::traits::inherit_default_bodies
  ```

  The duplicated `(impl_path, method)` is `into_raw_value` — the one `Address` method
  that carries a `#[verus_spec]` on its **trait declaration** (`result as int == self@`,
  in `src/libs/sys/src/sys/mm/address/mod.rs`).

- **Isolation performed**:
  - Trivial vs. real `from_address` spec: irrelevant (panic is from the trait impl,
    not `from_address`, which lives in the separate inherent impl).
  - Removing the trait-decl `#[verus_spec]` on `into_raw_value`: panic persists when the
    generic trait impl is `#[verus_verify]`'d (duplicate appears for the generic impl).
  - **Non-generic control**: adding `#[verus_verify]` to `impl Address for PhysicalAddress`
    (non-generic) does **not** panic (it proceeds to an unrelated `Unsupported constant
    type` error). ⇒ the trigger is the **generic** trait impl, not the spec itself.

- **Impact**: `PageAligned::into_raw_value`'s impl body cannot be machine-verified in this
  Verus version. Its **contract is still provided** to callers via the trait declaration
  spec (trait-method ensures are inherited by all impls). The impl is left unverified
  (trusted) — deliberately **not** `external_body` (which is forbidden here and not in
  `tcb-allowed.md`). Body is the trivial projection `self.0.into_raw_value()`.

- **Discharge plan**: the proving phase (or an upgraded Verus that fixes the
  `inherit_default_bodies` duplicate-registration assertion) should re-add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the `Address for PageAligned<T>` impl and confirm
  `result as int == self@` proves from `view() == self.0@` plus the inner
  `T::into_raw_value` trait spec.

- **Status**: open (tool bug). No Nanvix source logic is wrong.

---

## Proving-phase update (2026-06-15)

### VERUS-TOOL-1 — re-confirmed (still open)

Reproduced the `vir/src/traits.rs:511` panic with Verus `0.2026.05.24.ecee80a`
(the pinned, newest-available binary). Both alternatives were tried and rejected:

- Annotating only the method (`#[verus_verify]` on `fn into_raw_value`) is
  rejected: *"In order to verify any items of this trait impl, the entire impl
  must be verified."*
- Annotating the whole `impl` block panics Verus (duplicate `TraitMethodImpl`
  registration for `into_raw_value`).

I also empirically confirmed the body is currently **unverified**: replacing it
with `{ let _ = self.0.into_raw_value(); 0 }` (which violates `result as int ==
self@`) still reports `2 verified, 0 errors`. The body is therefore trusted via
the *trait-declaration* contract only — the impl body is not machine-checked.

Outcome: left unchanged and unannotated (no `admit`/`assume`/`external_body`).
Full reproduction, isolation, and mitigation moved to
`verus-unsupported.md` in this directory. This remains a Verus tool bug; no
Nanvix source logic is wrong.

## Improvement — eliminated an out-of-TCB trust boundary (not a bug)

**What**: `page.spec.rs` previously modeled `::arch::mem::PAGE_ALIGNMENT` with an
`assume_specification` (ensures `spec_align_value(PAGE_ALIGNMENT) ==
spec_page_size()`). `PAGE_ALIGNMENT` is **not** in `tcb-allowed.md`, so this was
an unlisted trust axiom that `from_address` depended on.

**Fix**: `PAGE_ALIGNMENT` is the concrete constant `Alignment::Align4096`. Adding
`#[verus_verify]` to its definition in
`src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/constants.rs` (matching the existing pattern on
`PAGE_SIZE` / `FRAME_SIZE`) lets Verus resolve the value directly, so
`spec_align_value(Align4096) == 4096 == PAGE_SIZE == spec_page_size()` is proved
rather than assumed. The `assume_specification` block was removed. `from_address`
still verifies (now with no trust axiom). This strengthens — never weakens — the
spec.

**Auto-Fixed**: Yes — added `#[verus_verify]` to the `PAGE_ALIGNMENT` constant
and deleted the `assume_specification` from `page.spec.rs`. Module verifies
`2 verified, 0 errors`; full `make verify` reports `0 errors` across all crates.

# Caller Analysis: `PageAligned` (`hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.rs`)

## Script Output

See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-hal-page-aligned/find_callers_lsp_output.md`
(raw output of `scripts/find_callers_lsp.py`).

Crate: `kernel` (no cross-crate dependents — intra-crate analysis only).
17 exec functions, all public/trait-pub, 0 private, 1 type (`PageAligned`).

In-scope (verification-order) targets, the only functions analyzed for design here:
`PageAligned::into_raw_value`, `PageAligned::from_address`, and the type `PageAligned`.

## Script Validation Notes (corrections / enrichment)

The LSP script reported `into_raw_value` as having **0 external callers**. This is a
**false negative**: `into_raw_value` is the `Address` trait method, and the script does
not resolve trait-method dispatch on concrete `PageAligned<_>` receivers. Real callers
found by reading the code:

- `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs:120` —
  `FrameAddress::into_raw_value(self)` returns `self.0.into_raw_value()`, where
  `self.0: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`. This is the **upstream verified caller**.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/elf.rs:288` —
  `let page_addr: usize = vaddr.into_raw_value();` with
  `vaddr: PageAligned<VirtualAddress>`.
- `page.rs:191` (internal) — `into_physical_address` calls `self.into_raw_value()`.

`from_address` results (19 external + 5 internal call sites) are accurate. The most
important caller is `FrameAddress::from_raw_value` (frame.rs:100), the upstream verified
boundary.

## Trait Obligations

- Trait `Address` for `PageAligned<T>` — `PageAligned` is itself an `Address`. The two
  in-scope trait/inherent functions must honor the `Address` contract:
  - `into_raw_value(self) -> usize`: pure projection to the underlying raw address value;
    no mutation, no failure. Must equal the abstract address (`self@`).
  - `from_address(addr: T) -> Result<Self, Error>` (inherent constructor; also the body of
    the `Address::from_raw_value` impl): validates page alignment and wraps `addr`.
- Trait `Deref for PageAligned<T>` (Target = `T`) — implicit; lets callers transparently use
  the inner address' methods. Not in scope but explains why many "uses" are auto-deref.

## Caller Expectations

### `PageAligned::from_address(addr: T) -> Result<Self, Error>`

Callers (frame.rs, elf.rs, region.rs, vmem.rs, identity_map.rs, boot_init.rs,
page_table.rs, page_directory.rs, process/manager, plus internal `from_raw_value`,
`align_up`, `align_down`, `into_physical_address`, `into_virtual_address`):

- Callers assume on **`Ok(self)`**: the wrapped address is page-aligned, i.e.
  `result@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (`result.inv()` holds). The value is preserved —
  `result@ == addr@` (no rounding; `from_address` rejects rather than aligns).
  - This is exactly what the upstream verified `FrameAddress::from_raw_value`
    (frame.rs:91-101) relies on: its spec ensures `Ok(fa) => fa.inv()`, delegating to
    `PageAligned::from_address`. Since `FrameAddress@ == PageAligned@`, `from_address`
    must guarantee `inv()` on success.
- Callers assume on **`Err`**: the input was not page-aligned (or the inner conversion
  failed); no `PageAligned` is produced. Most callers propagate with `?`.
- Callers don't care about: the concrete `Error`/`ErrorCode` payload, the exact alignment
  mechanism (`is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`), or that the value is stored as a tuple field.
- What would break callers: if `Ok` could be returned for an unaligned address, or if the
  stored value differed from the input (e.g. silent align-down). Both would invalidate the
  `inv()` guarantee the frame/region/vmem layers build on.

### `PageAligned::into_raw_value(self) -> usize`

Callers (`FrameAddress::into_raw_value` frame.rs:120, `elf.rs:288`, internal
`into_physical_address`):

- Callers assume the returned `usize` **equals the abstract address value** `self@`
  (the page-aligned raw address) — a faithful, total, side-effect-free projection.
  - The upstream `FrameAddress::into_raw_value` spec ensures `result as int == self@`,
    and its body is `self.0.into_raw_value()`. So `PageAligned::into_raw_value` must
    ensure `result as int == self@`.
- Because the receiver already satisfies `inv()`, callers may further assume the result is
  page-aligned (`result % page_size == 0`), though the core expectation is value equality.
- Callers don't care about: how the raw value is extracted from the inner `T`.
- What would break callers: returning anything other than `self@` (e.g. a shifted frame
  number, or a re-aligned value).

### Type `PageAligned<T>`

- 171 type references across the kernel (kframe, mmap, frame, mmio region, phys mm,
  process manager, vmem, elf, page tables…). Used as a **type-level proof of page
  alignment**: once a value has type `PageAligned<VirtualAddress>` /
  `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`, callers treat it as a guaranteed-aligned address and
  pass it without re-checking.
- `FrameAddress` wraps `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>` and derives both its `view`
  (`self.0@`) and `inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`) directly from it — so the
  `PageAligned` View/invariant is the foundation the frame layer is verified against.

## Abstract Resource

`PageAligned<T>` represents a **single memory address that is guaranteed to be aligned to a
page boundary** (a validated newtype over an `Address`). Its abstract value is just the
address (an `int`); its meaning is the carried proof that the address is page-aligned.

## Key Invariants (caller perspective)

- View: `PageAligned@ == (inner address)@` — abstract value is the raw address as `int`.
- Invariant: `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (`inv()`); every constructible `PageAligned`
  satisfies it.

   `FrameAddress::into_raw_value(self)` returns `self.0.into_raw_value()`, where

   `vaddr: PageAligned<VirtualAddress>`.
 - `page.rs:191` (internal) — `into_physical_address` calls `self.into_raw_value()`.

 important caller is `FrameAddress::from_raw_value` (frame.rs:100), the upstream verified

 ## Trait Obligations
 
 - Trait `Address` for `PageAligned<T>` — `PageAligned` is itself an `Address`. The two
   in-scope trait/inherent functions must honor the `Address` contract:
   - `into_raw_value(self) -> usize`: pure projection to the underlying raw address value;

   - `from_address(addr: T) -> Result<Self, Error>` (inherent constructor; also the body of

   the inner address' methods. Not in scope but explains why many "uses" are auto-deref.

 ### `PageAligned::from_address(addr: T) -> Result<Self, Error>`
 
 Callers (frame.rs, elf.rs, region.rs, vmem.rs, identity_map.rs, boot_init.rs,

   `result@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (`result.inv()` holds). The value is preserved —

   (the page-aligned raw address) — a faithful, total, side-effect-free projection.
   - The upstream `FrameAddress::into_raw_value` spec ensures `result as int == self@`,

   page-aligned (`result % page_size == 0`), though the core expectation is value equality.
 - Callers don't care about: how the raw value is extracted from the inner `T`.
 - What would break callers: returning anything other than `self@` (e.g. a shifted frame
   number, or a re-aligned value).
 
 ### Type `PageAligned<T>`
 
 - 171 type references across the kernel (kframe, mmap, frame, mmio region, phys mm,
   process manager, vmem, elf, page tables…). Used as a **type-level proof of page
   alignment**: once a value has type `PageAligned<VirtualAddress>` /
   `PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`, callers treat it as a guaranteed-aligned address and
   pass it without re-checking.

   (`self.0@`) and `inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`) directly from it — so the
   `PageAligned` View/invariant is the foundation the frame layer is verified against.

 `PageAligned<T>` represents a **single memory address that is guaranteed to be aligned to a
 page boundary** (a validated newtype over an `Address`). Its abstract value is just the
 address (an `int`); its meaning is the carried proof that the address is page-aligned.

 - View: `PageAligned@ == (inner address)@` — abstract value is the raw address as `int`.
 - Invariant: `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (`inv()`); every constructible `PageAligned`

   layer (and the wider `mm` stack) depends on; their guarantees must match
   `FrameAddress`'s existing specs (`Ok => fa.inv()`, `result == self@`).

 - `page.spec.rs` / `page.proof.rs` exist but are empty (`verus! { }`).

   View<V = int>>`:

   - `inv(&self) == self@ % spec_page_size() == 0` (open spec).
 - The in-scope functions `from_address` and `into_raw_value` currently have **no
   `#[verus_spec]`** annotations.
 - Upstream `FrameAddress` (frame.rs) already carries specs that *depend on* this module and
   are marked `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` "until the address layer is verified":
   - `from_raw_value` ensures `Ok(fa) => fa.inv()`.
   - `into_raw_value` ensures `result as int == self@`.
 
 ### Assessment
 
 - Coverage: **partial** — only the View + `inv` exist; the two target functions are
   unspecified.
 - Strength: the View/`inv` design is **adequate and caller-abstract** (value = address,
   invariant = page alignment); it already matches how `FrameAddress` models itself.
 - View design: **caller-abstract**, not biased — `FrameAddress` mirrors it verbatim,
   confirming `int` + page-alignment invariant is the right abstraction.
 - Action for verification: add specs to `from_address`
   (`Ok(r) => r@ == addr@ && r.inv()`) and `into_raw_value` (`result as int == self@`) so
   the `external_body` shims on `FrameAddress` can eventually be discharged. Do **not** add
   `external_body` to these in-scope functions unless listed in
   `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`.

24.     type V = int;
25. 
26.     // `closed`: callers may reference self@, but the mapping to the inner
27.     // field is hidden. The abstract value is "the address as an int".

30.     }
31. }
32. ```
33.

35. verified `FrameAddress` mirrors (`FrameAddress@ == self.0@`, where
36. `self.0 : PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`), confirming the abstraction is
37. caller-driven, not implementation-driven.

40.

42. to a caller-observable abstract concept, and there is only one here — the address.

44. per-value state, so it belongs in `inv()`, not the View. Wrapping a lone `int` in a
45. one-field struct would add ceremony to every spec with no gain in expressiveness.
46.

49. ## Well-formedness Invariant
50. 
51. ```rust
52. impl<T: Address + View<V = int>> PageAligned<T> {
53.     // `open`: callers (FrameAddress, region, vmem, page tables) must be able to
54.     // read and rely on the page-alignment fact directly in their own proofs.
55.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
56.         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
57.     }
58. }
59. ```
60. 
61. `inv()` states the one carried property: **every constructible `PageAligned`
62. value is page-aligned**. This is the proof obligation `from_address` must
63. establish and the fact `FrameAddress::inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`)
64. delegates to.
65. 
66. ---
67. 
68. ## Spec Transition Functions
69. 
70. `PageAligned` is an immutable validated newtype: neither in-scope function mutates
71. state. The "transitions" are therefore relations between an input address value
72. and the resulting abstract value, expressed as spec helpers on the View's `int`
73. domain.
74. 
75. ```rust
76. // Success condition for the validating constructor, stated purely on the
77. // abstract address value. `from_address` validates, it does NOT normalize:
78. // success requires the *input* to already be page-aligned.
79. pub open spec fn spec_aligned(addr_view: int) -> bool {

81. }

84. ### `from_address(addr: T) -> Result<Self, Error>` — validating constructor
85. 
86. ```text
87. ensures
88.     match result {
89.         Ok(r)  => spec_aligned(addr@) && r@ == addr@ && r.inv(),
90.         Err(_) => !spec_aligned(addr@),
91.     }

93. 
94. - **Value-preserving, not rounding**: `Ok(r) => r@ == addr@`. The address is
95.   carried through unchanged; an unaligned input is *rejected* (`Err`), never
96.   silently aligned down/up.

98.   layer (`FrameAddress::from_raw_value`, region, vmem) builds on.
99. - **Bidirectional failure**: `Err <=> !spec_aligned(addr@)`. The error condition is
100.   the abstract negation of the success condition, not a list of code checks; the
101.   concrete `Error`/`ErrorCode` payload is deliberately unconstrained (callers don't
102.   inspect it — they propagate with `?`).
103. 
104. ### `into_raw_value(self) -> usize` — total projection
105. 
106. ```text
107. ensures
108.     result as int == self@
109. ```
110.

112. - Matches the upstream `FrameAddress::into_raw_value` spec (`result as int ==

115.   `result % spec_page_size() == 0`, but value-equality is the core promise; no
116.   separate clause is needed (it is implied by `inv(self)` + this ensures).
117. 
118. ---
119. 
120. ## Design Rationale (per the substitution test)
121. 
122. > *If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different algorithm,
123. > would this still make sense?*
124. 
125. **Abstract value `self@ : int` = the raw aligned address.** ✅ Survives rewrite.
126. If `PageAligned` stored a frame index (`addr >> page_shift`), a tuple
127. `(base, offset)`, or any other encoding, the *address it denotes* is unchanged, so
128. `view() -> int` (the address) is still the right abstraction. `into_raw_value`'s
129. callers (`elf.rs:288`, `FrameAddress::into_raw_value`) consume this as a byte
130. address `usize`, so the View must denote the address, not an internal encoding.
131. 
132. **Invariant `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`.** ✅ Survives rewrite. Page alignment
133. is the defining property of *any* `PageAligned`, independent of how the value is
134. stored or how `from_address` checks it (`is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`, a mask, a
135. modulo). It is the single guarantee 171 type-reference sites rely on.
136. 
137. **`from_address` modeled as validate-and-preserve.** ✅ The contract
138. (`Ok => r@ == addr@`, `Err <=> unaligned`) is declarative: it pins *what*
139. (reject-or-preserve) without prescribing *how* the alignment test is performed.
140. Swapping the check mechanism leaves the spec valid.
141. 
142. Both `view` and `inv` already exist in the source and the analysis judges them
143. **adequate and caller-abstract**; this design ratifies them and supplies the two
144. missing function-level transitions so the `external_body` shims on `FrameAddress`
145. can eventually be discharged.
146. 
147. ---
148. 
149. ## Quality Review
150. 
151. | Criterion | Result |
152. |-----------|--------|
153. | **Substitution** | ✅ `int` address + page-alignment `inv` both survive a full reimplementation. |
154. | **Caller-only** | ✅ Address value and "is page-aligned" are exactly what callers reason about; no inner-field, `Error` payload, or check-mechanism leaks. |
155. | **Complete** | ✅ The two caller-observable concepts (the address; its alignment) are both represented; `from_address`/`into_raw_value` specs cover every caller expectation in the analysis. |
156. | **Minimal** | ✅ One scalar value + one invariant; `self@` is used by both target specs and by `FrameAddress`; `inv()` is used by `from_address` and all downstream layers. |

161. ## Rejected Alternatives
162. 
163. - **View as a frame index (`self.0@ / spec_page_size()`).** Rejected: callers
164.   (`into_raw_value` at `elf.rs:288`, `FrameAddress::into_raw_value`) expect the
165.   raw byte **address**, not a frame number. A frame-index View would force every
166.   caller to multiply back by the page size and would mismatch `FrameAddress`'s
167.   existing `self@`-as-address model. Fails *direct usability*.
168. 
169. - **A multi-field struct `{ addr: int, alignment: int }`.** Rejected: `alignment`
170.   is the module constant `spec_page_size()`, not per-value caller-observable state.
171.   Encoding it as a field would duplicate a constant into every value and complicate
172.   every spec. It belongs in `inv()`. Fails *minimal*.
173. 
174. - **A `bool is_aligned` field in the View.** Rejected: it would always be `true`

176.   invariant. Fails *minimal* / *no redundant fields*.

178. - **Exposing the inner `T` (e.g. `view() -> T::V` nested, or a `PhysicalAddress`
179.   wrapper).** Rejected: `T: View<V = int>` already collapses to `int`; surfacing

182.   `PhysicalAddress` and `VirtualAddress` instantiations need.
183.

187.   `Ok` be returned for an unaligned input with a silently changed value, breaking

189.   *sufficient to reject bugs*.

194.   substitution test.

197. 
198. To state `@`-based specs on generic functions over `T: Address` (e.g.

200. generic parameter must satisfy `T: View<V = int>`. Adding that bound only on the
201. `impl Address for PageAligned<T>` block cascades and breaks generic users such as
202. `MemoryRegion<PageAligned<T>>` in `region.rs`. The only non-cascading fix is to make
203. `View<V = int>` a **supertrait** of `Address`:

206. pub trait Address
207. where
208.     Self: core::fmt::Debug + Clone + PartialEq + Eq + PartialOrd + Ord + View<V = int>,

218.     to a plain `verus!{}` block.
219.   - `PageAligned` (kernel): `View` impl in a plain `verus!{}` block; `inv()` stays
220.     gated (it references `spec_page_size()`, a ghost-only `uninterp spec fn`).
221.   - `PageTableAligned` (kernel): new plain `verus!{}` `View` impl + `external_derive`.

223.   `Address` trait method in `sys`, so every implementor inherits it.

226. 
227. `PageAligned::into_raw_value` is the `Address` trait method. Its contract
228. `result as int == self@` lives on the trait declaration in `sys` and is therefore
229. inherited by `PageAligned`'s impl, giving callers (frame.rs, elf.rs) the guarantee.
230.

236. (`impl Address for PhysicalAddress`) does not panic. See `bugs.md`. The impl is therefore
237. left unverified (trusted) — *not* `external_body` — and its trivial body
238. (`self.0.into_raw_value()`) is left for the proving phase / a fixed Verus to discharge.

241. 
242. `from_address` no longer uses `proof!{admit();}` — it is fully discharged by two added
243. dependency specs:
244. 
245. - **`Address::is_aligned` trait spec** (`sys/mm/address/mod.rs`):
246.   `result matches Ok(aligned) && aligned == (self@ % spec_align_value(align) == 0)`.
247.   Guarantees `Ok` (every concrete impl always returns `Ok`), and relates the boolean to
248.   `self@` and the alignment value. Needed so `from_address`'s `Err => !spec_aligned(addr@)`
249.   arm holds (an `Err`-able `is_aligned` would let an aligned input propagate `Err`).
250. - **`spec_align_value(align: Alignment) -> int`** (`sys/mm/alignment.rs`, concrete `match`
251.   over the enum's byte values).
252. - **`PAGE_ALIGNMENT` model** (`page.spec.rs`) now links the constant to the page size:
253.   `spec_align_value(PAGE_ALIGNMENT) == spec_page_size()`. This is the explicit
254.   `PAGE_ALIGNMENT ↔ spec_page_size()` connection that lets `is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`
255.   prove `spec_aligned(addr@)`.
256. 
257. Only `into_raw_value` remains trusted (via the `Address` trait-decl spec) due to the
258. documented VERUS-TOOL-1 generic-trait-impl panic; `from_address` is now machine-proven.

 - **Bidirectional failure**: `Err <=> !spec_aligned(addr@)`. The error condition is
   the abstract negation of the success condition, not a list of code checks; the
   concrete `Error`/`ErrorCode` payload is deliberately unconstrained (callers don't
   inspect it — they propagate with `?`).
 
 ### `into_raw_value(self) -> usize` — total projection
 
 ```text
 ensures
     result as int == self@
 ```
 
 - A faithful, total, side-effect-free projection of the abstract address.
 - Matches the upstream `FrameAddress::into_raw_value` spec (`result as int ==
   self@`), whose body is literally `self.0.into_raw_value()`.
 - Because the receiver already satisfies `inv()`, callers may additionally derive
   `result % spec_page_size() == 0`, but value-equality is the core promise; no
   separate clause is needed (it is implied by `inv(self)` + this ensures).
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale (per the substitution test)
 
 > *If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different algorithm,
 > would this still make sense?*
 
 **Abstract value `self@ : int` = the raw aligned address.** ✅ Survives rewrite.
 If `PageAligned` stored a frame index (`addr >> page_shift`), a tuple
 `(base, offset)`, or any other encoding, the *address it denotes* is unchanged, so
 `view() -> int` (the address) is still the right abstraction. `into_raw_value`'s
 callers (`elf.rs:288`, `FrameAddress::into_raw_value`) consume this as a byte
 address `usize`, so the View must denote the address, not an internal encoding.
 
 **Invariant `self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`.** ✅ Survives rewrite. Page alignment
 is the defining property of *any* `PageAligned`, independent of how the value is
 stored or how `from_address` checks it (`is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`, a mask, a
 modulo). It is the single guarantee 171 type-reference sites rely on.
 
 **`from_address` modeled as validate-and-preserve.** ✅ The contract
 (`Ok => r@ == addr@`, `Err <=> unaligned`) is declarative: it pins *what*
 (reject-or-preserve) without prescribing *how* the alignment test is performed.
 Swapping the check mechanism leaves the spec valid.
 
 Both `view` and `inv` already exist in the source and the analysis judges them
 **adequate and caller-abstract**; this design ratifies them and supplies the two
 missing function-level transitions so the `external_body` shims on `FrameAddress`
 can eventually be discharged.
 
 ---
 
 ## Quality Review
 
 | Criterion | Result |
 |-----------|--------|
 | **Substitution** | ✅ `int` address + page-alignment `inv` both survive a full reimplementation. |
 | **Caller-only** | ✅ Address value and "is page-aligned" are exactly what callers reason about; no inner-field, `Error` payload, or check-mechanism leaks. |
 | **Complete** | ✅ The two caller-observable concepts (the address; its alignment) are both represented; `from_address`/`into_raw_value` specs cover every caller expectation in the analysis. |
 | **Minimal** | ✅ One scalar value + one invariant; `self@` is used by both target specs and by `FrameAddress`; `inv()` is used by `from_address` and all downstream layers. |
 | **No code-as-spec** | ✅ `inv` is a modulo predicate, not the `is_aligned` algorithm; `from_address` spec is a relation on `addr@`, not a transcription of the validation body. |
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 - **View as a frame index (`self.0@ / spec_page_size()`).** Rejected: callers
   (`into_raw_value` at `elf.rs:288`, `FrameAddress::into_raw_value`) expect the
   raw byte **address**, not a frame number. A frame-index View would force every
   caller to multiply back by the page size and would mismatch `FrameAddress`'s
   existing `self@`-as-address model. Fails *direct usability*.
 
 - **A multi-field struct `{ addr: int, alignment: int }`.** Rejected: `alignment`
   is the module constant `spec_page_size()`, not per-value caller-observable state.
   Encoding it as a field would duplicate a constant into every value and complicate
   every spec. It belongs in `inv()`. Fails *minimal*.
 
 - **A `bool is_aligned` field in the View.** Rejected: it would always be `true`
   (guaranteed by `inv()`), so it carries no information and is subsumed by the
   invariant. Fails *minimal* / *no redundant fields*.
 
 - **Exposing the inner `T` (e.g. `view() -> T::V` nested, or a `PhysicalAddress`
   wrapper).** Rejected: `T: View<V = int>` already collapses to `int`; surfacing
   the wrapper type would leak the newtype's internal layering without adding any
   caller-visible concept. The address-as-`int` View is the common denominator both
   `PhysicalAddress` and `VirtualAddress` instantiations need.
 
 - **Modeling `from_address` as normalizing (align-down on input).** Rejected: the
   caller analysis is explicit that `from_address` *validates, not normalizes*
   (`Ok(r) => r@ == addr@`; unaligned inputs `Err`). A normalizing model would let
   `Ok` be returned for an unaligned input with a silently changed value, breaking
   the `inv()`-preservation that `FrameAddress`/region/vmem depend on. Fails
   *sufficient to reject bugs*.
 
 - **Leaving the `Error` payload constrained (e.g. `Err(BadAddress)`).** Rejected as
   over-specification: no caller inspects the variant (all propagate with `?`).
   Pinning it would couple callers to an implementation detail and fail the
   substitution test.
 
 ## Implementation note: `Address: View<V = int>` supertrait (added this phase)
 
 To state `@`-based specs on generic functions over `T: Address` (e.g.
 `from_address`'s `addr@`, and `into_raw_value`'s `result as int == self@`), the
 generic parameter must satisfy `T: View<V = int>`. Adding that bound only on the
 `impl Address for PageAligned<T>` block cascades and breaks generic users such as
 `MemoryRegion<PageAligned<T>>` in `region.rs`. The only non-cascading fix is to make
 `View<V = int>` a **supertrait** of `Address`:
 
 ```rust
 pub trait Address
 where
     Self: core::fmt::Debug + Clone + PartialEq + Eq + PartialOrd + Ord + View<V = int>,
 ```
 
 Consequences (all applied this phase):
 - Every `Address` implementor must also implement `View<V = int>` in **normal**
   (non-Verus) builds, because the supertrait bound is a real Rust bound. `int`
   (`verus_builtin::int`, re-exported via `vstd::prelude::*`) is a real type in normal
   builds and the `verus!{}` View bodies are erased, so this compiles in both modes.
   - `VirtualAddress` (sys): already had a plain `verus!{}` `View` impl.
   - `PhysicalAddress` (kernel): `View` impl un-gated from `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`
     to a plain `verus!{}` block.
   - `PageAligned` (kernel): `View` impl in a plain `verus!{}` block; `inv()` stays
     gated (it references `spec_page_size()`, a ghost-only `uninterp spec fn`).
   - `PageTableAligned` (kernel): new plain `verus!{}` `View` impl + `external_derive`.
 - `into_raw_value`'s contract (`result as int == self@`) is declared once, on the
   `Address` trait method in `sys`, so every implementor inherits it.
 
 ## Implementation note: `into_raw_value` verification is tool-blocked (trusted via trait spec)
 
 `PageAligned::into_raw_value` is the `Address` trait method. Its contract
 `result as int == self@` lives on the trait declaration in `sys` and is therefore
 inherited by `PageAligned`'s impl, giving callers (frame.rs, elf.rs) the guarantee.
 
 We could not additionally *verify* `PageAligned`'s impl body against that contract:
 marking `impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T>` with `#[verus_verify]` triggers a
 Verus internal panic (`vir/src/traits.rs:511: assertion failed: !method_impls.contains(&p)`,
 duplicate `TraitMethodImpl` for `into_raw_value`). The panic is specific to a **generic**
 trait impl whose trait method carries a `#[verus_spec]`; the analogous non-generic impl
 (`impl Address for PhysicalAddress`) does not panic. See `bugs.md`. The impl is therefore
 left unverified (trusted) — *not* `external_body` — and its trivial body
 (`self.0.into_raw_value()`) is left for the proving phase / a fixed Verus to discharge.
 
 ## Update (turn 1 fix): `from_address` proven without `admit`
 
 `from_address` no longer uses `proof!{admit();}` — it is fully discharged by two added
 dependency specs:
 
 - **`Address::is_aligned` trait spec** (`sys/mm/address/mod.rs`):
   `result matches Ok(aligned) && aligned == (self@ % spec_align_value(align) == 0)`.
   Guarantees `Ok` (every concrete impl always returns `Ok`), and relates the boolean to
   `self@` and the alignment value. Needed so `from_address`'s `Err => !spec_aligned(addr@)`
   arm holds (an `Err`-able `is_aligned` would let an aligned input propagate `Err`).
 - **`spec_align_value(align: Alignment) -> int`** (`sys/mm/alignment.rs`, concrete `match`
   over the enum's byte values).
 - **`PAGE_ALIGNMENT` model** (`page.spec.rs`) now links the constant to the page size:
   `spec_align_value(PAGE_ALIGNMENT) == spec_page_size()`. This is the explicit
   `PAGE_ALIGNMENT ↔ spec_page_size()` connection that lets `is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`
   prove `spec_aligned(addr@)`.
 
 Only `into_raw_value` remains trusted (via the `Address` trait-decl spec) due to the
 documented VERUS-TOOL-1 generic-trait-impl panic; `from_address` is now machine-proven.

 - **A multi-field struct `{ addr: int, alignment: int }`.** Rejected: `alignment`
   is the module constant `spec_page_size()`, not per-value caller-observable state.
   Encoding it as a field would duplicate a constant into every value and complicate
   every spec. It belongs in `inv()`. Fails *minimal*.
 
 - **A `bool is_aligned` field in the View.** Rejected: it would always be `true`
   (guaranteed by `inv()`), so it carries no information and is subsumed by the
   invariant. Fails *minimal* / *no redundant fields*.
 
 - **Exposing the inner `T` (e.g. `view() -> T::V` nested, or a `PhysicalAddress`
   wrapper).** Rejected: `T: View<V = int>` already collapses to `int`; surfacing
   the wrapper type would leak the newtype's internal layering without adding any
   caller-visible concept. The address-as-`int` View is the common denominator both
   `PhysicalAddress` and `VirtualAddress` instantiations need.
 
 - **Modeling `from_address` as normalizing (align-down on input).** Rejected: the
   caller analysis is explicit that `from_address` *validates, not normalizes*
   (`Ok(r) => r@ == addr@`; unaligned inputs `Err`). A normalizing model would let
   `Ok` be returned for an unaligned input with a silently changed value, breaking
   the `inv()`-preservation that `FrameAddress`/region/vmem depend on. Fails
   *sufficient to reject bugs*.
 
 - **Leaving the `Error` payload constrained (e.g. `Err(BadAddress)`).** Rejected as
   over-specification: no caller inspects the variant (all propagate with `?`).
   Pinning it would couple callers to an implementation detail and fail the
   substitution test.
 
 ## Implementation note: `Address: View<V = int>` supertrait (added this phase)
 
 To state `@`-based specs on generic functions over `T: Address` (e.g.
 `from_address`'s `addr@`, and `into_raw_value`'s `result as int == self@`), the
 generic parameter must satisfy `T: View<V = int>`. Adding that bound only on the
 `impl Address for PageAligned<T>` block cascades and breaks generic users such as
 `MemoryRegion<PageAligned<T>>` in `region.rs`. The only non-cascading fix is to make
 `View<V = int>` a **supertrait** of `Address`:
 
 ```rust
 pub trait Address
 where
     Self: core::fmt::Debug + Clone + PartialEq + Eq + PartialOrd + Ord + View<V = int>,
 ```
 
 Consequences (all applied this phase):
 - Every `Address` implementor must also implement `View<V = int>` in **normal**
   (non-Verus) builds, because the supertrait bound is a real Rust bound. `int`
   (`verus_builtin::int`, re-exported via `vstd::prelude::*`) is a real type in normal
   builds and the `verus!{}` View bodies are erased, so this compiles in both modes.
   - `VirtualAddress` (sys): already had a plain `verus!{}` `View` impl.
   - `PhysicalAddress` (kernel): `View` impl un-gated from `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`
     to a plain `verus!{}` block.
   - `PageAligned` (kernel): `View` impl in a plain `verus!{}` block; `inv()` stays
     gated (it references `spec_page_size()`, a ghost-only `uninterp spec fn`).
   - `PageTableAligned` (kernel): new plain `verus!{}` `View` impl + `external_derive`.
 - `into_raw_value`'s contract (`result as int == self@`) is declared once, on the
   `Address` trait method in `sys`, so every implementor inherits it.
 
 ## Implementation note: `into_raw_value` verification is tool-blocked (trusted via trait spec)
 
 `PageAligned::into_raw_value` is the `Address` trait method. Its contract
 `result as int == self@` lives on the trait declaration in `sys` and is therefore
 inherited by `PageAligned`'s impl, giving callers (frame.rs, elf.rs) the guarantee.
 
 We could not additionally *verify* `PageAligned`'s impl body against that contract:
 marking `impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T>` with `#[verus_verify]` triggers a
 Verus internal panic (`vir/src/traits.rs:511: assertion failed: !method_impls.contains(&p)`,
 duplicate `TraitMethodImpl` for `into_raw_value`). The panic is specific to a **generic**
 trait impl whose trait method carries a `#[verus_spec]`; the analogous non-generic impl
 (`impl Address for PhysicalAddress`) does not panic. See `bugs.md`. The impl is therefore
 left unverified (trusted) — *not* `external_body` — and its trivial body
 (`self.0.into_raw_value()`) is left for the proving phase / a fixed Verus to discharge.
 
 ## Update (turn 1 fix): `from_address` proven without `admit`
 
 `from_address` no longer uses `proof!{admit();}` — it is fully discharged by two added
 dependency specs:
 
 - **`Address::is_aligned` trait spec** (`sys/mm/address/mod.rs`):
   `result matches Ok(aligned) && aligned == (self@ % spec_align_value(align) == 0)`.
   Guarantees `Ok` (every concrete impl always returns `Ok`), and relates the boolean to
   `self@` and the alignment value. Needed so `from_address`'s `Err => !spec_aligned(addr@)`
   arm holds (an `Err`-able `is_aligned` would let an aligned input propagate `Err`).
 - **`spec_align_value(align: Alignment) -> int`** (`sys/mm/alignment.rs`, concrete `match`
   over the enum's byte values).
 - **`PAGE_ALIGNMENT` model** (`page.spec.rs`) now links the constant to the page size:
   `spec_align_value(PAGE_ALIGNMENT) == spec_page_size()`. This is the explicit
   `PAGE_ALIGNMENT ↔ spec_page_size()` connection that lets `is_aligned(PAGE_ALIGNMENT)`
   prove `spec_aligned(addr@)`.
 
 Only `into_raw_value` remains trusted (via the `Address` trait-decl spec) due to the
 documented VERUS-TOOL-1 generic-trait-impl panic; `from_address` is now machine-proven.

1. # Verus-Unsupported Constructs — `kernel::hal::mem::types::address::aligned::page`
2. 
3. This file records a Verus tool limitation hit while verifying the `page` module.
4. It is an **internal Verus assertion panic**, not a Nanvix code bug and not a
5. proof gap. No exec code was changed and no `external_body` was added to work
6. around it (the function is not in `tcb-allowed.md`).
7. 
8. ## 1. Verifying a generic trait impl panics Verus (`inherit_default_bodies`)
9. 
10. ### Where
11. `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.rs`
12. 
13. ```rust
14. impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T> {
15.     fn into_raw_value(self) -> usize { self.0.into_raw_value() }
16.     // ... clone_address, from_raw_value, align_up, align_down,
17.     //     is_aligned, max_addr, as_ptr, as_mut_ptr
18. }
19. ```
20. 
21. To machine-verify the body of `PageAligned::into_raw_value` against its trait
22. contract (`result as int == self@`) the **whole** trait impl must be annotated
23. (`#[verus_verify]` on the `impl` block). Verus does not allow annotating a single
24. method of a trait impl:
25. 
26. ```
27. error: In order to verify any items of this trait impl, the entire impl must be
28. verified. Try wrapping the entire impl in the `verus!` macro.
29. ```
30. 
31. ### Exact error (when the `impl` block is annotated `#[verus_verify]`)
32. ```
33. thread 'rustc' panicked at vir/src/traits.rs:511:13:
34. assertion failed: !method_impls.contains(&p)
35. ...
36. vir::traits::inherit_default_bodies
37. error: could not compile `kernel` (bin "kernel")
38. ```
39. 
40. The duplicated `(impl_path, method)` key is `into_raw_value` — the only `Address`
41. method that takes `self` **by value** and whose trait declaration carries a
42. `#[verus_spec]` referencing `self@` (`src/libs/sys/src/sys/mm/address/mod.rs`).
43. 
44. ### Minimal trigger / isolation
45. - Trigger is the **generic** trait impl: annotating the non-generic
46.   `impl Address for PhysicalAddress` does *not* panic (it proceeds past this
47.   point). The generic `impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T>` (and the
48.   structurally identical `impl<T: Address> Address for PageTableAligned<T>` in
49.   `pgtab.rs`) does panic.
50. - Removing the trait-declaration `#[verus_spec]` on `into_raw_value` does **not**
51.   avoid the panic — the duplicate `TraitMethodImpl` registration for the generic
52.   impl still occurs during HIR→VIR lowering.
53. - Verus version: `0.2026.05.24.ecee80a` (pinned in `build/verus-version`; the
54.   newest binary available on this machine). Older local binaries
55.   (`0.2026.05.13`) are not newer and were not tried as a downgrade.
56. 
57. ### Why it is unsupported
58. The assertion is inside `inherit_default_bodies`, which builds the set of
59. `(impl_path, trait_method)` pairs from `krate.functions`. For this generic trait
60. impl Verus registers two `FunctionKind::TraitMethodImpl` entries with the same
61. key for `into_raw_value`, violating the `assert!(!method_impls.contains(&p))`
62. invariant. This is an internal verifier bug — there is exactly one user-written
63. `impl Address for PageAligned` in the crate (confirmed by grep), so the duplicate
64. is generated by Verus, not by the source.
65. 
66. ### Mitigation (no trust boundary introduced)

 It is an **internal Verus assertion panic**, not a Nanvix code bug and not a
 proof gap. No exec code was changed and no `external_body` was added to work
 around it (the function is not in `tcb-allowed.md`).
 
 ## 1. Verifying a generic trait impl panics Verus (`inherit_default_bodies`)
 
 ### Where
 `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/aligned/page.rs`
 
 ```rust
 impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T> {
     fn into_raw_value(self) -> usize { self.0.into_raw_value() }
     // ... clone_address, from_raw_value, align_up, align_down,
     //     is_aligned, max_addr, as_ptr, as_mut_ptr
 }
 ```

 contract (`result as int == self@`) the **whole** trait impl must be annotated
 (`#[verus_verify]` on the `impl` block). Verus does not allow annotating a single
 method of a trait impl:
 
 ```
 error: In order to verify any items of this trait impl, the entire impl must be
 verified. Try wrapping the entire impl in the `verus!` macro.
 ```
 
 ### Exact error (when the `impl` block is annotated `#[verus_verify]`)
 ```
 thread 'rustc' panicked at vir/src/traits.rs:511:13:
 assertion failed: !method_impls.contains(&p)
 ...
 vir::traits::inherit_default_bodies
 error: could not compile `kernel` (bin "kernel")
 ```

 method that takes `self` **by value** and whose trait declaration carries a
 `#[verus_spec]` referencing `self@` (`src/libs/sys/src/sys/mm/address/mod.rs`).
 
 ### Minimal trigger / isolation
 - Trigger is the **generic** trait impl: annotating the non-generic
   `impl Address for PhysicalAddress` does *not* panic (it proceeds past this
   point). The generic `impl<T: Address> Address for PageAligned<T>` (and the
   structurally identical `impl<T: Address> Address for PageTableAligned<T>` in
   `pgtab.rs`) does panic.
 - Removing the trait-declaration `#[verus_spec]` on `into_raw_value` does **not**
   avoid the panic — the duplicate `TraitMethodImpl` registration for the generic
   impl still occurs during HIR→VIR lowering.

   newest binary available on this machine). Older local binaries

---
name: ast-consistency
description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
---

# AST Consistency Check

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
| `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
| `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
| `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
| `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
| `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
| `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
| `v.std_method(args)` | `wrapper(&mut v, args)` | `&mut T` method unsupported; see `verus-constraints` skill for wrapper rules |

### Bug Fix Deviations

Exec changes that fix verified bugs are also pre-approved. These must:
- Have a `// VERUS BUG FIX: <description>` comment at the fix site
- Be recorded in `bugs.md` with full evidence
- Be committed with `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix
- Be limited to auto-fixable categories (overflow, off-by-one, missing
  bounds check, unchecked cast) — see `bug-reporting` skill

## Handling MISMATCHes

When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
   `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
   manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
   Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
   keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
   change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
   - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
   - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
   - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
4. **If confirmed, document with full evidence.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
   comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
   what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with

- **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
- **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
- **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation

- Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
- Anything requiring architectural changes
- Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches

---
name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not

---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
   strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
   functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
   (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
   record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
   the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
   `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
  in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
- **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
  cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
  `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |

## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost

- **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
- **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.

See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.

## Warnings

Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:

- **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
  the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
  choose triggers automatically.
- **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
  to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.

## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)

Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
`axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.

**Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search

after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
strengthen the proof, do not change the code.

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.
